content: Myocardial infarction and worsening of varicose veins are potential adverse effects. Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders may include urticaria and chloasma. Reproductive system and breast disorders may involve penile disorders, including localized reactions on the penis in male partners of women using the NuvaRing, as well as galactorrhea. Drug Interactions It is essential to review the labeling of all concurrently used medications to assess potential interactions with hormonal contraceptives or the likelihood of enzyme alterations. Substances that decrease the plasma concentrations of combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) may reduce their effectiveness. Drugs or herbal products that induce certain enzymes, such as cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), can lower plasma concentrations of CHCs, potentially diminishing their contraceptive efficacy or increasing the likelihood of breakthrough bleeding. Examples of such drugs or herbal products include phenytoin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, bosentan, felbamate, griseofulvin, oxcarbazepine, rifampicin, topiramate, rifabutin, rufinamide, aprepitant, and products containing St. John’s wort. Interactions between CHCs and other drugs may result in breakthrough bleeding and/or contraceptive failure. Women should be counseled to use an alternative or backup contraceptive method when enzyme inducers are used with the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring. Backup contraception should continue for 28 days after discontinuing the enzyme inducer to ensure contraceptive reliability. The serum concentrations of etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol are not affected by the concomitant administration of oral amoxicillin or doxycycline in standard dosages during 10 days of antibiotic treatment. However, the effects of other antibiotics on etonogestrel or ethinyl estradiol concentrations have not been evaluated. Substances Increasing Plasma Concentrations of CHCs Co-administration of atorvastatin and certain CHCs containing ethinyl estradiol increases the area under the curve (AUC) values for ethinyl estradiol by approximately 20-25%. Ascorbic acid and acetaminophen may increase plasma ethinyl estradiol concentrations, possibly by inhibiting conjugation. CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as itraconazole, voriconazole, fluconazole, grapefruit juice, or ketoconazole, may elevate plasma hormone concentrations. Co-administration of vaginal miconazole nitrate with the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring increases serum concentrations of etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol by up to 40%. CHCs have been shown to decrease plasma concentrations of acetaminophen, clofibric acid, morphine, salicylic acid, and temazepam. A significant reduction in plasma concentrations of lamotrigine has been observed, likely due to the induction of lamotrigine glucuronidation. This may reduce seizure control, necessitating dosage adjustments of lamotrigine. Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy Women on thyroid hormone replacement therapy may require increased doses of thyroid hormone because CHC use increases serum concentrations of thyroid-binding globulin. Laboratory Test Interference The use of contraceptive steroids may influence the results of certain laboratory tests, including coagulation factors, lipids, glucose tolerance, and binding proteins. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy According to the FDA, there is little or no increased risk of birth defects in women who inadvertently use CHCs during early pregnancy. Epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have not found an increased risk of genital or non-genital birth defects (including cardiac anomalies and limb-reduction defects) following exposure to low-dose CHCs prior to conception or during early pregnancy. CHCs should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. The administration of CHCs to induce withdrawal bleeding should not be used as a test for pregnancy. Labor and Delivery There is no FDA guidance on the use of etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring during labor and delivery. Nursing Mothers The effects of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring in nursing mothers have not been evaluated and remain unknown. When possible, nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. CHCs can reduce milk production in breastfeeding mothers. This is less likely to occur once breastfeeding is well-established, but it can happen at any time in some women. Small amounts of contraceptive steroids and/or their metabolites are present in breast milk. Pediatric Use The safety and efficacy of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring have been established in women of reproductive age. Efficacy is expected to be the same for postpubertal adolescents under the age of 18 and for users aged 18 years and older. Use of this product before menarche is not indicated. Geriatric Use The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring has not been studied in postmenopausal women and is not indicated for this population. Gender There is no FDA guidance on the use of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring with respect to specific gender populations. Race There is no FDA guidance on the use of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring with respect to specific racial populations. Renal Impairment The effect of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring has not been studied. Hepatic Impairment The effect of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring has not been studied. Steroid hormones may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function. Acute or chronic disturbances of liver function may necessitate the discontinuation of CHC use until liver function markers return to normal.
